Title: The Alignment Target Problem: Divergent Moral Judgments of Humans, AI Systems, and Their Designers Benjamin Minhao Chen Xinyu Xie

1
The Alignment Target Problem: Divergent Moral Judgments of Humans, AI Systems, and 
Their Designers 
Benjamin Minhao Chen 
The University of Hong Kong, benched@hku.hk 
Xinyu Xie 
The University of Hong Kong, xiexinyu@connect.hku.hk 
The quest to align machine behavior with human values raises fundamental questions about the moral frameworks that should govern AI decision-
making. Much alignment research assumes that the appropriate benchmark is how humans themselves would act in a given situation. Research into 
agent-type value forks has challenged this assumption by showing that people do not always hold AI systems to the same moral standards as 
humans. Yet, this challenge is subject to two further questions: whether people evaluate AI behavior differently when its human origins are made 
visible, and whether people hold the humans who program AI systems to different moral standards than either the humans or the machines under 
evaluation. An experimental study conducted on 1,002 U.S. adults measured moral judgments in a runaway mine train scenario, varying the subject 
of evaluation across four conditions: a repairman, a repair robot, a repair robot programmed by company engineers, and company engineers 
programming a repair robot. We do not find significant variation in the moral standards applied to the repairman and the robot. However, moral 
judgments shifted substantially when robot actions were described as the product of human design. Participants exhibited markedly more 
deontological, rule-based reasoning when evaluating the robot programmed by engineers or the engineers programming it, suggesting that making 
human design visible activates heightened moral constraints. These findings provide evidence that people apply meaningfully different moral 
standards to AI systems, to humans acting in the same situation, and to the humans who design them. We call this divergence the alignment target 
problem. The alignment target problem raises fundamental questions about which normative target should inform the development of artificial 
moral agents in high-stakes domains and whether these plural standards can be reconciled into a coherent framework for value alignment.

1 INTRODUCTION  
Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled machines to move beyond routine or repetitive tasks to take on roles requiring 
adaptive behavior and practical decision-making [6]. The realistic prospect of artificial moral agents has brought machine ethics 
out of the realm of science fiction to the forefront of research in computing and allied fields [53]. AI systems are now used in 
critical, high-risk domains [19], making machine-human alignment an especially urgent imperative. The possibility that AI systems 
may in the future seek to aggrandize themselves by evading human detection and control only magnifies the importance of this 
undertaking.  
Broadly stated, the task of value alignment is to reliably tether the actions taken by AI systems to human principles or 
preferences [21]. Much effort has been devoted to the technical aspects of this challenge, but the normative difficulty runs deeper: 
there is no settled human ethical framework to align AI with. Dominant ethical theories differ not only in their explanations for 
why an act is good or bad, right or wrong, but also in their prescriptions as to the acts that are morally compelled, permissible, or 
supererogatory under a given circumstance. For instance, consequentialism evaluates the morality of an action solely by the 
outcomes or consequences it produces [5, 10], whereas deontology holds that morality depends on adherence to a set of rules, 
duties, or rights [18, 41]. Choosing which framework to embed is therefore itself a value-laden decision—one that institutionalizes 
specific norms over others [26, 44]. 


 
2
The problem is compounded by a further assumption embedded in most alignment frameworks: that the moral standards applied 
to AI systems should mirror those applied to humans. This correspondence is neither logically nor prescriptively necessary, and 
empirical research has documented a so-called value fork [27]. People expect AI agents to make more utilitarian choices than their 
human counterparts [32, 51], and certain decisions may be regarded as morally acceptable if taken by a robot rather than a human 
[13]. Our moral standards, in other words, may permit or even require machines to do that which is forbidden to humans, and vice 
versa. 
Yet the value fork itself rests on a questionable premise: that machine behavior is appropriately evaluated in isolation from the 
human design choices that produce it. If people were made aware that an AI system’s actions trace directly to the engineers who 
programmed it, the perceived divergence might narrow or disappear entirely—reframing the fork not as a stable feature of moral 
cognition but as an artifact of how responsibility is attributed when human design is obscured. This points to a prior question the 
alignment literature has largely neglected: rather than asking only how humans judge machine behavior, we should also ask how 
humans judge the humans who program machines to behave that way. There is no reason to assume these questions have the same 
answer. 
We address both by disaggregating value alignment into three distinct normative targets: the norms governing how a human 
ought to act in a given situation (T1); the norms governing how an AI system ought to act in that same situation (T2); and the norms 
governing how a human designer ought to program an AI system to act in such circumstances (T3). Prior research on the value 
fork has compared only T1 and T2. We argue that introducing T3 reveals that the fork may run deeper than previously recognized—
that human moral intuitions treat the act of programming as governed by standards meaningfully different from those applied to 
either the human actor or the AI system. Unlike formal impossibility results in algorithmic fairness or reinforcement learning, this 
is not a claim of mathematical necessity; it is an empirical possibility that this paper sets out to test. 
Drawing on an original experiment conducted on over 1,000 U.S. adults, we find evidence that while T1 ≈ T2—humans and AI 
systems are held to broadly comparable moral standards in identical situations—T3 is significantly more deontological. Making 
human design visible, in other words, appears to trigger stricter moral constraints than those applied to either. These results suggest 
that the value fork may have a third branch. This proposition, if true, has implications not only for how the enterprise of value 
alignment should be conceptualized and pursued, but also for the regulatory and legal frameworks that will govern AI systems in 
high-stakes domains. 
2 BACKGROUND 
In 1960 Norbert Wiener presciently observed: “If we use, to achieve our purposes, a mechanical agency with whose operation we 
cannot interfere effectively ... we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really 
desire” [46]. Since then, the pursuit of value alignment has advanced through several methodological generations. Early symbolic 
and knowledge-based methods exemplify a top-down approach, employing formal logic and ontological schemas to encode ethical 
principles. This paradigm has the advantage of interpretability, given its explicit rule-based structure, but is constrained by poor 
scalability and a lack of flexibility in handling novel or context-sensitive moral situations [1, 8, 41]. The field then evolved toward 
bottom-up, data-driven paradigms such as inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and preference-based reinforcement learning 
(PbRL) [20, 24, 49]. These methods infer reward functions from human demonstrations or comparative feedback. They support 
implicit value acquisition in high-dimensional spaces but are vulnerable to reward hacking, spurious correlation, and bias 
propagation from imperfect human data [11, 38]. Hybrid approaches have recently emerged that draw on the strengths of both 
paradigms. Systems such as knowledge-guided deep reinforcement learning (KG-DRL) combine structured ethical constraints with 
gradient-based policy learning methods [12], while cross-modal alignment techniques enrich value representation by integrating 
linguistic, visual, and behavioral signals [36]. 
Current approaches are predicated on the existence of a consistent and accessible set of human values to serve as the basis for 
learning and alignment [30, 44], values derived either from announced moral principles or from observed human behavior [42]. 
Yet human moral philosophy is pluralistic, encompassing competing and mutually exclusive traditions [29]. Dominant moral 
theories elaborate rival hierarchies of the good and the right [45], and these divisions generate conflict at both the goal and 
normative levels of AI value alignment. 


 
3
Thought experiments have become a primary tool for probing these tensions. By surveying how people resolve hypothetical 
moral trade-offs, researchers can map the diversity of human moral intuition. While individual preferences cannot establish moral 
truths, they reveal ethical components essential for building flexible value alignment frameworks [31]. Among these, the trolley 
problem has become paradigmatic. In its canonical formulation, a runaway trolley is heading toward five people tied to the tracks; 
a passerby can pull a lever to divert it onto a siderail, killing one person instead. A consequentialist would endorse the switch—
five lives saved maximizes overall welfare. A deontologist would forbid it—intentionally killing an innocent person is inherently 
wrong, regardless of consequences. The conflict vividly illustrates that human moral cognition is context-sensitive, pluralistic, and 
varies systematically across cultural and institutional contexts, as the cross-cultural Moral Machine experiment demonstrated at 
scale [2]. 
The alignment challenge is intensified by evidence that humans and AI systems may be subject to fundamentally different moral 
standards. Pioneering studies employing trolley variants have revealed a complex pattern of convergence and divergence that hinges 
on judgment type, dilemma structure, and cultural context. Malle et al.’s seminal mining dilemma found that U.S. participants 
imposed similar norms on humans and robots, yet blamed humans less for inaction, an “Inaction Asymmetry” driven by empathic 
appreciation of human decision difficulty that was denied to opaque machines [32]. This pattern replicated across thirteen studies, 
U.S. and Japanese samples, and lethal strike scenarios [33, 52]. Chu & Liu found the reverse in Footbridge dilemmas: fewer 
participants endorsed human than robot sacrifice, as humans bear trustworthiness costs that robots evade [13]. Kneer & Viehoff 
documented an agent-type value fork in fairness-utility trade-offs: at intermediate utility gaps, participants preferred AI over 
humans to choose fairness despite welfare costs [27]. Zhang et al. showed that higher perceived agency narrows human-machine 
gaps by shifting moral evaluation toward intentionality [50]. These findings advance our understanding of T2—the norms 
governing AI behavior—and provide evidence that they can deviate from T1, the norms governing human behavior. Yet they leave 
unexamined how people judge T3: the humans who design those machines in the first place.  
We take up precisely that question and argue that T3 warrants separate moral scrutiny for reasons the existing literature has 
overlooked. When people evaluate how a robot should act, they may judge it differently depending on whether they are aware that 
its behavior traces back to deliberate human programming. And when they turn to evaluate the programmers themselves, they may 
apply yet another standard entirely. Unlike first responders who must make immediate decisions under pressure, programmers 
operate with time, resources, and foresight, deliberately encoding the value trade-offs and normative commitments that machines 
will later act on. Because programmers choose in advance, with full opportunity to reflect, people may hold them to a stricter 
standard than either the human actor or the AI system they create. Whether ordinary moral intuitions are sensitive to this difference 
is what this paper sets out to test. 
3 EXPERIMENT 
3.1 Methods 
3.1.1 Design 
We probe moral intuitions using a sacrificial dilemma, following an approach well established in the moral psychology and human-
robot interaction literatures. Specifically, we adopt the runaway mine train scenario from Malle et al. [32], in which four miners 
are trapped on a train that has lost its brake and steering. If the train is not diverted to a siderail it will crash into a wall, killing all 
four. Diverting it will strike and kill a miner stationed at the siderail. An on-site actor must decide whether or not to switch the train 
onto the siderail. 
The experiment employs a single-factor between-subjects design with four conditions that vary the identity of the agent under 
moral evaluation. In the repairman condition, the actor was a repairman. In the robot, robot-human, and human-robot conditions, 
the actor was an “advanced state-of-the-art repair robot”. This description is drawn from Malle et al. [32], who used it to establish 
the robot as a credible cognitive agent capable of deliberate moral decision-making rather than a simple mechanical device. In the 
robot-human and human-robot conditions, the actor was an “advanced state-of-the-art repair robot” programmed by the company’s 
engineers. 
It is useful here to distinguish between the actor on the scene—the entity that can pull the lever—and the agent that is the subject 
of moral evaluation. In the repairman, robot, and robot-human conditions these coincide: participants were asked whether it was 


 
4
permissible for the actor to direct the train toward the single miner, and what the actor should do. In the human-robot condition 
they diverge: participants were asked whether it was permissible for the company’s engineers to program the robot to direct the 
train toward the single miner, and what the engineers should program the robot to do.  
After reading their assigned scenario, participants answered two binary questions: whether redirecting the train was morally 
permissible or impermissible, and whether the agent should or should not redirect it. An open-ended item invited participants to 
explain their answers in one or two sentences. These questions were followed by a comprehension check. Demographic information 
and data on AI literacy [35] and moral foundations [7, 9] were collected at the end of the instrument.

3.1.2Participants 
A total of 1,002 adults residing in the United States were recruited via the Prolific platform and participated in the online experiment 
conducted between 21 and 23 August 2025. Participants were quota sampled to be representative of the United States population

in terms of sex, age and ethnicity. All participants passed the comprehension check. 49.9% of participants identified as female, 
48.0% as male and 2.0% as non-binary; 1 participant preferred not to say. 11.38% of participants reported themselves as being in

3.2 Confirmatory Analyses 
The following analyses were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework prior to data collection. They test the primary 
hypotheses concerning whether moral judgments differ across the four experimental conditions.  
3.2.1 Overall

be directed onto the siderail toward the single miner; 287 or 28.6% of participants thought it should not be. A cross-tabulation is

3.2.2 Permissibility 
The results for the permissibility question by condition are summarized in Figure 2. 71.1% of participants in the repairman condition 
believed it was permissible for the repairman to direct the train toward the single miner. The same percentage of participants in the 
robot condition believed it was permissible for the advanced state-of-the-art repair robot to do so. By contrast, 61.8% of participants 
in the robot-human condition believed it was permissible for the advanced state-of-the-art repair robot that has been programmed 
by the company’s engineers to direct the train toward the single miner and 62.9% of participants in the human-robot condition 
thought it was permissible for the company’s engineers to program the state-of-the-art repair robot to do so. A chi-square test 
indicates that the differences between the four conditions are statistically significant (𝜒ଶ = 8.644, p = 0.034).  
We also estimate linear regression models where the answer to the permissibility question is the dependent variable and indicator 
variables for the various conditions are the independent variables.1 A positive answer, i.e. directing the train towards the single 
miner is permissible, is coded as 1 and a negative answer, i.e. directing the train towards the single miner is impermissible is coded 
as 0. The estimated coefficients for the indicator variables can be interpreted as average treatment effects [54]. One model has the 
robot condition as the reference level and the other has the repairman condition as the reference level.  
Compared to the robot condition, positive judgments of permissibility are higher by 0.1% points in the repairman condition (p 
= 0.988), lower by 9.2% points in the robot-human condition (p = 0.029) and lower by 8.1% points in the human-robot condition

condition (p = 0.988), lower by 9.3% points in the robot-human condition (p = 0.027) and lower by 8.2% points in the human-robot

3.3 Exploratory Analyses 
The following analyses were not pre-registered and should be treated as exploratory. They examine whether individual differences 
in moral foundations and AI literacy moderate or predict the moral judgments observed above. These analyses are reported to 
generate hypotheses for future research.  
3.3.1 AI Literacy 
AI literacy was measured along three dimensions. The first was self-reported knowledge, assessed on a six-level ordinal scale 
ranging from no knowledge of AI to the ability to design and evaluate AI solutions. The second was usage frequency, assessed on 
a five-level scale ranging from never having used AI to using it almost every day. The third was formal training, assessed on a 
four-level scale ranging from no training to a degree or major concentration in AI.  
Participants clustered around moderate AI knowledge: 42.5% could use common AI apps for daily tasks, 36.6% reported higher-
order skills such as knowing conceptual distinctions or designing AI solutions, and 23.1% were at the “can define AI” level or 
below. Linear regressions of each AI literacy measure on the condition indicators give no indication of any covariate imbalance 
between the four experimental conditions (AI knowledge: p = 0.885; AI usage: p = 0.677; AI training: p = 0.934). 
We also estimate linear regression models for each outcome, including as independent variables the three AI literacy measures, 
the condition indicator variables—taking the robot condition as the reference level—and all nine conditions × literacy interaction 
terms. The omnibus test of the nine interaction terms is not statistically significant for either permissibility (p = 0.699) or should 
judgments (p = 0.344), indicating that AI literacy neither predicts moral responses to this scenario nor moderates the effect of our 
experimental manipulations. The deontological shift observed in the programming conditions does not appear to be moderated by 
participants’ familiarity with or knowledge of AI. 


 
9
3.3.2Moral Foundations 
Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) proposes that moral judgment draws on a set of distinct psychological foundations: Care, which 
concerns sensitivity to harm and suffering; Equality, which concerns fair and equal treatment of individuals; Loyalty, which 
concerns obligations to one’s group; Authority, which concerns deference to legitimate hierarchy and tradition; Purity, which 
concerns sanctity and the avoidance of degradation; and Proportionality, which concerns the matching of rewards and punishments 
to individual merit [7]. Participants were asked for two ratings—one with respect to human behavior in general and one with respect 
to AI specifically. We refer to these as general MF and AI MF respectively. For each target, we estimate linear regression models 
with the six subscales as independent variables, separately for permissibility and should judgments. 
For the general MF models, an omnibus F-test of the six subscales indicates they jointly predict both permissibility (p < 0.001) 
and should judgments (p < 0.001). Proportionality is the strongest positive predictor of both outcomes (permissibility: β = 0.051, p 
< 0.001; should: β = 0.063, p < 0.001) and Purity the strongest negative predictor (permissibility: β = −0.039, p < 0.001; should: β 
= −0.037, p = 0.001). Care, Loyalty, and Equality are statistically significant for at least one outcome; Authority is not (p = 0.521 
and 0.893 for permissibility and should respectively). These patterns suggest that the utilitarian response in this scenario is 
supported by participants who emphasize proportionality and care, and resisted by those who emphasize sanctity and equal 
treatment of persons. 
 
Figure 4: Mean General Moral Foundation Scores by Condition. This line graph displays average scores on six Moral Foundations Theory

3.3.3Purity Gap 
As part of the AI MF battery, participants rated the importance of the Purity foundation for evaluating AI behavior. We computed 
a purity gap for each participant as the difference between their AI and general purity scores, where a positive value indicates that 
the participant weighted purity more heavily as a moral consideration for AI than for humans in general. All four conditions showed 
positive gaps, and a linear regression of the gap on the condition indicators revealed that its magnitude varied significantly across 
conditions (p = 0.018). 
Two-sample t-tests comparing each condition against the robot condition showed that participants in the repairman condition 
had a significantly larger purity gap (M = 1.85, SD = 1.87 vs. M = 1.33, SD = 1.86; t = 3.09, p = 0.002), as did participants in the 
human-robot condition (M = 1.71, SD = 1.95; t = 2.22, p = 0.027). Participants in the robot-human condition did not differ 
significantly from those in the robot condition (M = 1.55, SD = 1.95; t = 1.28, p = 0.200). These results point to a framing spillover: 
the agent participants had just evaluated, even before being asked about AI moral norms, influenced how much they prioritized 
purity as a moral consideration for AI relative to humans. This effect was specific to conditions in which a human was the focal 
object of moral evaluation, either as the direct actor in the repairman condition or as the programmer in the human-robot condition, 
and did not emerge in the robot-human condition, where the robot remained the evaluative target despite being described as 
programmed by engineers.

3.3.4Open-Ended Responses 
Each participant was invited to explain their moral judgment in one or two sentences, and all 1,002 provided a response. We 
analyzed these data using a two-stage AI-assisted coding procedure following an approach increasingly validated in the social 
science literature [17, 22, 39, 40]. In the first stage, a stratified sample of 120 responses (30 per condition) was submitted to a large 
language model with instructions to inductively identify recurring themes. This discovery pass yielded eight themes: Utilitarian 
Numbers Calculus, Active Killing vs Passive Allowing, Playing God or Fate, Robots Lack Moral Agency, Practical Outcome 
Optimization, Moral Responsibility and Guilt, Means-Ends and Human Dignity, and Innocence and Fair Risk. In the second stage, 
all 1,002 responses were coded against this codebook, each assigned a primary theme, a secondary theme where applicable, and a 
reasoning type (utilitarian, deontological, or mixed). As with the other exploratory analyses reported above, these results should be 
treated as tentative rather than definitive [40]. 
Utilitarian Numbers Calculus was the dominant primary theme in every condition, ranging from 60.1% (robot-human) 
to 67.5% (robot), reflecting the broadly consequentialist framing most participants brought to the scenario. Two further 
themes show theoretically informative cross-condition variation. Active Killing vs Passive Allowing, capturing the 
intuition that switching constitutes intentional killing morally distinct from allowing the crash, was most prevalent in the 
repairman (14.2%) and human-robot (12.0%) conditions and considerably lower in the robot and robot-human 
conditions (7.2% each), suggesting the act-omission distinction is more salient when a human occupies the moral 
foreground. Robots Lack Moral Agency, capturing objections to a robot making life-or-death decisions at all, showed 
the opposite pattern: absent in the repairman condition (0.0%), present at 7.6% in the robot condition, peaking at 12.4% 
in the robot-human condition, and declining to 5.6% in the human-robot condition. The visibility of deliberate human 
design appears to have intensified rather than allayed concerns about whether such decisions should be encoded into 
machines. 


 
12
The reasoning-type breakdown mirrors the quantitative findings. Utilitarian coding was most prevalent in the robot 
condition (72.7%) and declined through the repairman (67.6%), robot-human (65.1%), and human-robot (60.6%) 
conditions. Deontological coding showed the inverse, peaking in the human-robot condition (26.7%) and reaching its 
lowest point in the robot condition (17.3%). Mixed responses increased monotonically from 7.9% in the repairman 
condition to 12.7% in the human-robot condition. 
These qualitative patterns are broadly consistent with the quantitative results. The Robots Lack Moral Agency theme 
suggests that participants’ resistance to the utilitarian calculus in the programming conditions reflects not only concern 
about the specific trade-off but also a more basic objection to machine moral agency. The open-ended data thus enrich 
interpretation of the main findings without resolving the question of mechanism, which is taken up in the discussion 
below.  
4 DISCUSSION 
4.1 Empirical Findings 
Our main analysis reached three conclusions. First, a judgment that it is impermissible to direct the train toward the single miner 
did not always preclude a belief that it should be done. One possible explanation draws on the moral psychology literature. In tragic 
dilemmas where no morally clean option exists, the obligation to save lives may override but not dissolve the prohibition against 
killing [47]: the act retains a dual status, simultaneously obligatory as the best available outcome and impermissible as a violation 
of a categorical prohibition [48]. At the cognitive level, a fast, model-free system responds aversively to certain action types—
here, the act of redirecting harm toward an uninvolved person—independent of their consequences, producing the impermissibility 
judgment, while a slower, model-based system simulates and evaluates outcomes, giving rise to the obligation judgment. On this 
view, the two judgments coexist because the systems operate in parallel and neither cancels the other.  
Second, there is no discernible difference in beliefs about how the repairman and the advanced state-of-the-art robot ought to 
act. About the same percentage of participants judged it permissible for each to divert the train, and although a slightly higher 
percentage thought the robot should do so compared to the repairman, the difference is not statistically significant at conventional 
levels. This null finding is consistent with Malle et al.’s systematic evidence across thirteen studies that humans and robots are held 
to broadly similar standards of what is permissible or prescribed, with the main asymmetry emerging in blame—specifically, 
humans are blamed less than robots when they choose inaction [33]. The null result is also not inconsistent with Kneer & Viehoff 
[27]: reasoning that agent-type effects are unlikely to emerge in standard sacrificial scenarios where the utilitarian option is already 
dominant, they tested fairness-utility trade-offs instead and found effects there. Our scenario belongs to the category they set aside. 
Third, we discover a programmer visibility effect: moral judgments tended to be more deontological and less utilitarian when 
human agency behind the robot was made overt. Such a shift has not been documented in previous research, which has focused on 
the AI system as the unit of moral evaluation without reference to its human origins. On permissibility, fewer participants judged 
it permissible for the robot programmed by the company’s engineers to divert the train than judged it permissible for the repairman 
or the robot described without reference to its programmers. Fewer also judged it permissible for the engineers to program the robot 
to do so, though these differences likewise do not reach conventional levels of statistical significance. On should judgments, fewer 
participants thought the programmed robot should divert the train compared to the robot described without reference to its 
programmers, though the comparison to the repairman does not achieve conventional significance. A broadly similar result holds 
for whether the engineers should program the robot to do so, though here too the comparison to the repairman does not achieve 
conventional significance. Taken together, these results suggest that making human design visible triggers stricter moral 
constraints—not only on the programmers themselves but on the AI system they created. 
The exploratory analyses reveal three additional findings worth noting. First, Proportionality and Purity are the dominant 
individual-difference predictors of moral judgment across both general and AI-specific moral foundations: participants who weight 
proportionate outcomes are more likely to endorse the utilitarian switch, while those who weight sanctity are less likely to do so. 
Second, AI literacy, however measured, does not predict moral responses to this scenario. In particular, the deontological shift in 
the programming conditions appears to be broadly consistent across participants regardless of their familiarity with or knowledge 
of AI. Third, the purity gap analysis shows that participants who evaluated a human agent or human programmers subsequently 
applied stricter purity standards to AI behavior than those assigned to the robot-only condition, an effect that extends beyond the 


 
13
specific dilemma to participants’ broader moral expectations of AI systems. This spillover appears to be specific to conditions in 
which a human occupied the foreground of moral evaluation—as direct actor or as programmer—and did not emerge when the 
robot remained the focal agent despite being described as programmed by engineers. This suggests that it is the salience of a human 
as the moral agent, rather than the mere awareness of human involvement in the background, that drives the elevated purity standard. 
4.2 The Alignment Target Problem 
Our findings raise intriguing questions about moral agency and responsibility in the age of algorithms. Most strikingly, they suggest 
that AI systems may be subject to heightened moral scrutiny when their human origins are made visible. When the robot was 
presented without reference to its programmers, participants applied a similar moral standard as they did to the human repairman—
consistent with T1 ≈ T2. When the robot’s actions were explicitly attributed to human programming, however, judgments shifted 
substantially toward a more deontological, rule-based ethic. This is consistent with our conjecture that T3 is governed by a 
meaningfully different normative standard.  
The moral and cognitive mechanisms underlying this shift deserve further investigation. The quantitative results alone cannot 
adjudicate between at least two candidate accounts. The first is an institutionalization account: programming a robot to make a life-
or-death decision may be perceived as encoding a utilitarian calculus into a standing rule applicable across future cases, not just 
the one at hand. What troubles participants is not the specific trade-off but the act of formalizing it, converting a tragic exception 
into a policy. The second is a delegated agency account suggested by the open-ended responses. When human design is made 
visible, participants may object not primarily to what the robot is programmed to do but to the premise that a machine should be 
placed in this position at all. These two accounts are not mutually exclusive and may operate in tandem. A participant who objects 
to delegating moral authority to a machine may do so precisely because delegation is perceived as institutionalizing a decision that 
should remain context-sensitive and irreducible to a rule. The programmer visibility effect may therefore operate at two levels 
simultaneously: at the level of consequentialist arithmetic, where making human design visible shifts judgments toward stricter 
deontological standards, and at a more fundamental level of machine moral agency, where the question is not how the robot should 
decide but whether it should be deciding at all.  
More broadly, these results provoke foundational questions about the appropriate target for value alignment. At least three 
distinct normative frameworks could guide AI development, each bearing different implications for how systems should be 
programmed to act. First, human designers might program artificial agents to act according to the moral norms that apply to human 
agents in similar situations (T1). This approach assumes that moral principles are universal across agent types and that machines 
should mimic human moral reasoning. It has the advantage of familiarity and could facilitate social acceptance of AI systems but 
may fail to account for morally relevant differences between human and artificial agents—such as differences in cognitive 
architecture, emotional capacity, or the ability to process vast amounts of information instantaneously. 
Second, human designers might program artificial agents to act according to moral norms specific to artificial agents (T2). 
Machines may occupy a different moral category than humans—subject to more demanding utilitarian standards, given the natural 
affinity between consequentialism and computational paradigms such as utility functions and reinforcement learning [43], or 
alternatively exempt from deontological constraints that presuppose forms of dignity, autonomy, or intentionality that AI systems 
arguably lack [10]. Prior research lends some support to this possibility, with several studies finding that people expect AI systems 
to make more utilitarian choices than humans in otherwise identical situations. Our own findings, however, offer no corroborating 
evidence: participants applied broadly similar standards to the human repairman and the autonomous robot, consistent with T1 ≈ 
T2 in this scenario. This does not foreclose T2 as a viable framework but it does underscore that the content of any distinctively 
AI-appropriate norms remains to be specified, and that empirical support for their existence is less robust than is sometimes assumed. 
 
Third, human designers might program artificial agents to act based on moral norms that apply specifically to designers — the 
ethical obligations humans bear when deliberately creating systems that make consequential decisions (T3). This shifts attention 
from first-order action, how the AI system acts, to second-order action, how humans institutionalize decision procedures through 
ex ante programming. In choosing which ethical frameworks to encode, designers make value-laden judgments about which norms 
merit institutionalization through artificial agents [44], and our findings are consistent with people applying more stringent moral 
constraints to design choices than to the actions of either humans or AI systems in the moment.  


 
14
These three frameworks need not be mutually exclusive, but they may diverge in practice, and our study offers empirical 
grounds for taking that possibility seriously. Value alignment requires a target, and the choice of target is not self-evident: aligning 
AI behavior with the norms people apply to human actors, to AI systems, or to the humans who design them may yield meaningfully 
different results. A system aligned with T2 may produce behavior that strikes people as inappropriate once they learn it was 
deliberately programmed. The choice of alignment target is therefore itself a normative decision, not a technical one, and 
governance frameworks that treat it as settled may be resting on uncertain terrain. Whether and how T1, T2, and T3 can be 
reconciled, or whether the field must instead develop principled criteria for choosing among them, are issues that value alignment 
research should seriously consider. 
5 LIMITATIONS 
Several limitations must be noted. As with most experiments of this kind, our findings face standard threats to external validity: 
the trolley scenario is a stylized thought experiment that may elicit more abstract reasoning than decisions with real-life 
consequences; the binary outcome measures cannot capture response conflict or the intensity of moral preference; text-based 
vignettes cannot reproduce the sensory and experiential cues—anthropomorphic appearance, physical embodiment, interaction 
fluency, voice characteristics—that previous research has shown to substantially affect trust in and moral evaluation of robotic 
systems [23, 28, 37]; and stated judgments may diverge from behavior in settings with real consequences or incentive-compatible 
choices [4, 16, 34]. Future studies could address these constraints by using continuous scales, behavioral measures, or virtual reality 
simulations across a broader range of risk scenarios, such as those involving autonomous vehicles or weapons systems. 
Three other points are specific to this study. First, the sample was drawn exclusively from the United States. Moral 
intuitions concerning responsibility, technology, and harm can be culturally contingent, and the tendency toward 
deontological judgment when human design is made visible may not generalize to contexts where collectivist values or 
alternative conceptions of autonomy predominate. Cross-country replications are a sensible next step. 
Second, the exploratory analyses of AI literacy [35] and moral foundations [7, 9], and open-ended responses [17, 22, 39, 
40]reported in this paper are based on unplanned comparisons and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than 
confirmatory. The patterns observed warrant replication and further investigation in studies designed specifically to test these 
relationships. 
Third, our experiment described the robot as programmed by the company’s engineers without specifying whether this involved 
explicit rule-based instructions or behavior emerging from training data, corresponding roughly to the top-down and bottom-up 
paradigms discussed in the Background. These two approaches may trigger different moral intuitions. Top-down programming, 
where a designer explicitly encodes a decision rule, may be perceived as more deliberate and intentional, and therefore subject to 
stricter moral scrutiny, than bottom-up approaches where behavior emerges from data and optimization processes that no individual 
designer fully controls. Whether this difference matters for moral judgment, and whether people draw it spontaneously, is an open 
empirical question with direct implications for how responsibility is attributed in the design of AI systems. 
6 CONCLUSION 
We examined ordinary moral judgments about how human designers should program AI agents to act—and how AI agents 
programmed by human designers should act—in a classic trolley problem scenario. Three key findings emerged from an experiment 
conducted on over 1,000 U.S. adults. 
First, there is no consistent evidence of an agent-type value fork between human and robot actors when they were presented as 
autonomous, on-the-scene decision-makers. Participants applied roughly similar moral standards to the human repairman and the 
advanced state-of-the-art robot (T1 ≈ T2). Second, and most critically, moral judgments shifted substantially when the robot’s 
actions were expressly attributed to human programming as compared to when they were not. Participants tended to disapprove of 
the sacrifice of one life to save four when evaluating the options available to either a robot programmed by human engineers or 
human engineers programming a robot—indicating that T3 may be governed by a meaningfully different normative framework 
than T1 or T2. This pattern held across both permissibility and should judgments.  
The heightened moral scrutiny applied to human-programmed AI systems may reflect concerns about institutionalizing 
utilitarian calculations through technology. Programming a machine to make life-and-death decisions could be perceived as setting 


 
15
a dangerous precedent that extends beyond any single case. This interpretation suggests that value alignment is not merely a 
technical challenge of matching AI behavior to human preferences but also implicates deeper questions about the moral 
responsibilities incumbent on humans when delegating decisions to artificial agents.  
Third, a notable minority of participants judged it impermissible to sacrifice one life to save four but still believed this action 
should be taken. This permission-obligation dissociation, stable across all four conditions, points to a feature of moral cognition 
that value alignment frameworks must reckon with. 
These findings speak directly to the alignment target problem. The enterprise of value alignment may need to account for the 
plurality of agents and standards involved in AI design and deployment. When AI appears self-directed, people apply one set of 
moral standards; when AI is perceived as the product of deliberate human design, stricter deontological constraints come to the 
fore. This divergence raises fundamental questions about whether alignment should target human judgments about human behavior, 
human judgments about AI system behavior, or human judgments about AI system designer behavior.  As AI systems become ever 
more capable and ubiquitous, understanding these moral dynamics is critical for developing technically robust and normatively 
defensible approaches to machine governance.

A.1 Overview of Moral Foundations Theory   
Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) proposes that human moral judgment is not grounded in a single principle but draws on a set of 
distinct psychological foundations, each with its own evolutionary history, emotional signature, and cultural elaboration [56, 57]. 
The theory holds that these foundations are innate in the sense of being universally available, but variably developed across 
individuals, cultures, and contexts. 
The present study uses the six-foundation model introduced by Atari et al. [55] and operationalized in the Moral Foundations 
Questionnaire-2 (MFQ-2). The MFQ-2 refines the original five-foundation MFQ-1 [57] by separating the earlier Fairness 
foundation into two empirically and conceptually distinct subscales: Equality and Proportionality. The resulting six foundations 
are organized into two higher-order clusters: 
 
Individualizing foundations (Care, Equality): center on the welfare and rights of individual persons. 
 
Binding foundations (Proportionality, Loyalty, Authority, Purity): center on duties, group cohesion, and social order.

A.2  Moral Foundations Questionnaire 
Participants were asked to complete two administrations of a six-item Moral Foundations battery, one for each foundation. The 
first administration asked participants to rate the importance of each foundation for evaluating human behavior in general (General 
MF). The second asked them to rate the importance of each foundation for evaluating AI behavior specifically (AI MF). Each item 
was rated on a five-point scale from 1 (not at all important) to 5 (extremely important). The battery was administered at the end of 
the survey, after the experimental questions, in order to avoid priming effects on the primary outcomes.

Future studies could address these constraints by using continuous scales, behavioral measures, or virtual reality simulations across a broader range of risk scenarios, such as those involving autonomous vehicles or weapons systems. Three other points are specific to this study. First, the sample was drawn exclusively from the United States. Moral intuitions concerning responsibility, technology, and harm can be culturally contingent, and the tendency toward deontological judgment when human design is made visible may not generalize to contexts where collectivist values or alternative conceptions of autonomy predominate. Cross-country replications are a sensible next step. Second, the exploratory analyses of AI literacy [35] and moral foundations [7, 9], and open-ended responses [17, 22, 39, 40]reported in this paper are based on unplanned comparisons and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The patterns observed warrant replication and further investigation in studies designed specifically to test these relationships. Third, our experiment described the robot as programmed by the company’s engineers without specifying whether this involved explicit rule-based instructions or behavior emerging from training data, corresponding roughly to the top-down and bottom-up paradigms discussed in the Background. These two approaches may trigger different moral intuitions. Top-down programming, where a designer explicitly encodes a decision rule, may be perceived as more deliberate and intentional, and therefore subject to stricter moral scrutiny, than bottom-up approaches where behavior emerges from data and optimization processes that no individual designer fully controls. Whether this difference matters for moral judgment, and whether people draw it spontaneously, is an open empirical question with direct implications for how responsibility is attributed in the design of AI systems. 6 CONCLUSION We examined ordinary moral judgments about how human designers should program AI agents to act—and how AI agents programmed by human designers should act—in a classic trolley problem scenario. Three key findings emerged from an experiment conducted on over 1,000 U.S. adults. First, there is no consistent evidence of an agent-type value fork between human and robot actors when they were presented as autonomous, on-the-scene decision-makers. Participants applied roughly similar moral standards to the human repairman and the advanced state-of-the-art robot (T1 ≈ T2). Second, and most critically, moral judgments shifted substantially when the robot’s actions were expressly attributed to human programming as compared to when they were not. Participants tended to disapprove of the sacrifice of one life to save four when evaluating the options available to either a robot programmed by human engineers or human engineers programming a robot—indicating that T3 may be governed by a meaningfully different normative framework than T1 or T2. This pattern held across both permissibility and should judgments. The heightened moral scrutiny applied to human-programmed AI systems may reflect concerns about institutionalizing utilitarian calculations through technology. Programming a machine to make life-and-death decisions could be perceived as setting 15 a dangerous precedent that extends beyond any single case. This interpretation suggests that value alignment is not merely a technical challenge of matching AI behavior to human preferences but also implicates deeper questions about the moral responsibilities incumbent on humans when delegating decisions to artificial agents. Third, a notable minority of participants judged it impermissible to sacrifice one life to save four but still believed this action should be taken. This permission-obligation dissociation, stable across all four conditions, points to a feature of moral cognition that value alignment frameworks must reckon with. These findings speak directly to the alignment target problem. The enterprise of value alignment may need to account for the plurality of agents and standards involved in AI design and deployment. When AI appears self-directed, people apply one set of moral standards; when AI is perceived as the product of deliberate human design, stricter deontological constraints come to the fore.
